content.text: De Quervain's tenosynovitis is an overuse condition, particularly of activities involving repeated ulnar deviation of the wrist. It occurs due to friction between the APL and EPB tendons within their sheath in the first dorsal compartment.
As with all tenosynovitis conditions, movement is the most provoking factor (as opposed to isometric load).

items: De Quervain's — pain felt distal to the extensor retinaculum
Intersection syndrome — pain felt proximal to the extensor retinaculum
Wartenberg syndrome — involves the superficial branch of the radial nerve, manifests as paresthesia

content.text: Treatment of all three is similar.

items: Gradual onset
Overuse of wrist, especially ulnar deviation and thumb movements
Paresthesia is NOT expected — its presence suggests Wartenberg syndrome
Is this a new activity, or recent change or sudden increase in activity?
AROM shows pain with ulnar deviation and flexion of the wrist and movements of the thumb
PROM is similar to AROM but may not be as provocative
RROM of APL & EPB is generally painful but not to the same extent as AROM (because in neutral position the tendons aren't moving through the irritated sheath)
Muscle weakness may occur in APL and EPB
MMT of these muscles may rule out muscle strain
Finkelstein test will be positive
Joint play assessment of the wrist may be helpful — if inadequate joint play for deviations is present, motions require greater muscle effort
Restoring ulnar glide and radial glide of the wrist may provide important pain relief
Identify and modify irritating activity (e.g. switch hands, use power tools instead of manual)
Orthoses to prevent ulnar deviation — more effective when combined with corticosteroid injection
Strengthening: symptom-free isometrics before progressing to isotonics
Exercises should use precise positioning given potential to increase tendon friction

content.text: If paresthesia is present, the person should avoid any compression over the wrist (jewellery, wrist bands). The radial nerve is the most superficial structure of the distal radial forearm and is highly susceptible to external compression.

items: Reduce adhesions around the tendon sheath
Promote normal resting muscle tone of the affected muscles
Promote normal joint play and reduced fascial restrictions in area
Treat compensatory structures to restore overall function
Reduce adhesions around APL & EPB tendon sheath with skin rolling and MFR
Promote normal resting muscle tone of APL & EPB using segmental muscle stripping, petrissage, and dynamic release
Maintain neuromuscular control with gentle isometric muscle setting
Decrease tension in posterior forearm with petrissage and work on superficial extensors
Restore normal joint play with radiocarpal mobilisations and carpal joint play
Reduce fascial restriction with intercompartmental MFR and deep MFR

content.title: Cautions
content.text: Do not friction or put direct pressure down into the affected tendon sheath. Avoid active or passive movement of the thumb unless clearly pain-free. Avoid heat directly over the tendon sheath which may be inflamed.
Provided that the provoking activities are identified and can be reduced or adequately modified, most people have symptoms resolved within 3-6 weeks.

quiz.question: Which special test is positive in De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
quiz.explanation: The Finkelstein test will be positive in De Quervain's tenosynovitis.

quiz.question: Which two tendons are affected in De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
quiz.explanation: De Quervain's involves friction between the Abductor Pollicis Longus (APL) and Extensor Pollicis Brevis (EPB) within their sheath in the first dorsal compartment.

quiz.question: If a patient with radial wrist pain reports paresthesia, which condition should be suspected?
quiz.explanation: Paresthesia is not expected in De Quervain's — its presence suggests Wartenberg syndrome, which involves the superficial branch of the radial nerve.
